source_text: Nos unum deum colimus, quem omnes naturaliter nostis, ad cujus fulgura et tonitrua contremiscitis, ad cujus beneficia gaudetis. Caeteros et ipsi putatis deos esse, quos nos daemonas scimus. Tamen humani juris et naturalis potestatis est unicuique, quod putaverit, colere; nec alii obest aut prodest, alterius religio. Sed nec religionis est cogere religionem, quae sponte suscipi debeat, non vi: cum et hostiae ab animo libenti expostulentur. Ita etsi nos compuleritis ad sacrificandum, nihil praestabitis diis vestris: ab invitis enim sacrificia non desiderabunt; nisi si contentiosi sunt; contensiosus autem deus non est. Denique qui est verus, omnia sua ex aequo et profanis et suis praestat. Ideoque et judicium constituit aeternum de gratis et ingratis. Tamen nos, quos sacrilegos existimatis, nec in furto unquam deprehendistis, nedum in sacrilegio. Omnes autem qui templa despoliant, et per deos jurant, et eosdem colunt, et christiani non sunt, et sacrilegi tamen deprehenduntur. Longum est si retexamus, quibus aliis modis et derideantur et contemnantur omnes dii, ab ipsis cultoribus suis. Sic et circa majestatem Imperatoris infamamur, tamen nunquam albiniani, nec nigriani, vel cassani inveniri potuerunt christiani: sed idem ipsi qui per genios eorum in pridie usque juraverunt, qui pro salute eorum hostias et fecerant et voverant, qui christianos saepe damnaverant, hostes eorum sunt reperti. Christianus nullius est hostis, nedum Imperatoris: quem sciens a Deo suo constitui, necesse est ut et ipsum diligat, et revereatur, et honoret, et salvum velit, cum toto romano imperio, quousque saeculum stabit. Tamdiu enim stabit. Colimus ergo et Imperatorem sic, quomodo et nobis licet, et ipsi expedit, ut hominem a Deo secundum, et quicquid est a Deo consecutum, solo Deo minorem. Hoc et ipse volet. Sic enim omnibus major est, dum solo vero Deo minor est: sic et ipsis diis major est, dum et ipsi in potestate sunt ejus. Itaque et sacrificamus pro salute Imperatoris, sed Deo nostro et ipsius: sed quomodo praecepit Deus, pura prece. Non enim eget Deus, conditor universitatis, odoris aut sanguinis alicujus. Haec enim daemoniorum pabula sunt. Daemones autem non tantum respuimus, verum et revincimus, et quotidie traducimus, et de hominibus expellimus, sicut plurimis notum est. Ita nos magis oramus pro salute Imperatoris, ab eo eam postulantes, qui praestare potest. Et utique ex disciplina patientiae divinae agere nos, satis manifestum esse vobis potest, cum tanta hominum multitudo, pars pene major civitatis cujusque, in silentio et modestia agimus, singuli forte noti magis quam omnes: nec aliunde noscibiles quam de emendatione vitiorum pristinorum. Absit enim ut indigne feramus ea nos pati quae optamus, aut ultionem a nobis aliquam machinemur, quam a Deo exspectamus.
pass_a_gloss: We worship one God, whom all naturally know, at whose lightning and thunder you tremble, at whose benefits you rejoice. The others, you also think are gods, whom we know are demons. Nevertheless, it is human right and natural power for each to worship what he thinks; nor does another's religion harm or benefit. But nor is it of religion to force religion, which ought to be undertaken spontaneously, not by force: since sacrifices are also demanded from a willing mind. Thus, even if you compel us to sacrifice, you will accomplish nothing for your gods: for sacrifices are not desired from unwilling ones; unless they are contentious; but God is not contentious. Finally, he who is true, provides all things equally to his own and to profane ones. And therefore he establishes eternal judgment concerning the grateful and the ungrateful. Nevertheless, we, whom you consider sacrilegious, you have never caught in theft, much less in sacrilege. But all who despoil temples, and swear by gods, and worship them, and are not Christians, are nevertheless caught in sacrilege. It would be long to recount in how many ways all gods are ridiculed and despised by their own worshipers. So also we are infamous concerning the majesty of the Emperor, nevertheless Christians have never been found to be Albiniani or Nigeriani or Cassiani: but the same ones who had sworn by their genii, who had made and vowed sacrifices for their safety, who had often condemned Christians, were found to be their enemies. A Christian is the enemy of no one, much less of the Emperor: whom, knowing to have been established by his God, it is necessary that he also love, and reverence, and honor, and wish to be safe, with the whole Roman empire, as long as the age stands. For it will stand that long. Therefore we worship the Emperor in such a way as is permitted to us, and is expedient for him, as a man second to God, and whatever is consequent upon God, less than God alone. This also he himself wants. For thus he is greater than all, while less than the true God alone: thus he is also greater than the gods, while they are in his power. And so we sacrifice for the safety of the Emperor, but to our God and his: but in the way God commanded, with pure prayer. For God, the founder of the universe, does not need the smell or blood of anything. For these are the food of demons. And demons we not only reject, but also overcome, and daily lead away, and expel from men, as is known to many. Thus we pray more for the safety of the Emperor, asking it from him who can provide it. And certainly it is manifest to you that we act from the discipline of divine patience, since such a multitude of men, almost the greater part of each city, act in silence and modesty, perhaps known individually more than all: nor are we known otherwise than from the correction of former vices. For it is far from us to bear unworthily what we suffer, which we desire, or to devise any vengeance, which we expect from God.
pass_b_english: We worship one God—the same God everyone knows by nature, whose lightning and thunder make you tremble, whose blessings make you rejoice. You call the others gods as well; we know them for demons. Still, it is a human right and a natural prerogative for each person to worship whatever he chooses; another's religion neither harms nor helps anyone else. But religion is not the business of coercion: true religion must be embraced freely, not forced, because sacrifice is demanded from a willing heart. So even if you compel us to offer sacrifices, you will accomplish nothing for your gods, since they do not accept offerings from unwilling people—unless they are quarrelsome, and God is not quarrelsome. In the end, the true God provides for all equally, both his own and the profane, and for that very reason he has established an eternal judgment to separate the grateful from the ungrateful.

Yet you label us sacrilegious, though you have never caught us in theft, let alone sacrilege. By contrast, every temple robber swears by your gods, worships them, is not a Christian—and yet gets caught in sacrilege. It would take too long to list all the ways your own worshipers ridicule and despise every one of your gods. Likewise we are slandered regarding the Emperor's majesty, but no Christian has ever been found among the Albiniani, the Nigeriani, or the Cassiani. Instead, the very men who swore by the Emperors' guardian spirits, who offered and vowed sacrifices for their safety, who had often condemned Christians—those men turned out to be the Emperors' enemies. A Christian is no one's enemy, much less the Emperor's: knowing that the Emperor was established by his God, a Christian must love, revere, honor him, and pray for his safety along with the whole Roman empire for as long as the world endures—and it will endure that long.

Therefore we honor the Emperor in the only way that is both lawful for us and profitable for him: as a man second only to God, and whatever he possesses as a gift from God, inferior to God alone. That is what the Emperor himself should want, because only by being less than the true God is he greater than all; only by having the so-called gods under his power is he greater than they. So we do offer sacrifice for the Emperor's safety, but to our God and his—and we do it as God commanded, with pure prayer. God, the Creator of the universe, does not need the smell or blood of anything; those are the food of demons. Demons we not only reject, we defeat, we lead away daily, we cast out of human beings, as many people know. That is why we pray all the more effectively for the Emperor's safety, asking it from the One who can actually grant it. And the fact that we act from the discipline of divine patience should be obvious to you: a vast multitude, nearly the majority in every city, lives in silence and modesty, known individually perhaps more than collectively, and recognized only by the reform of their former vices. It is utterly foreign to us to bear suffering unworthily—we desire this suffering—or to devise any vengeance of our own, because we expect justice from God.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex theological distinctions regarding the Emperor's status and the nature of sacrifice. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the original meaning without adding or omitting key arguments. All scripture-alluded concepts (though no direct verse citations were present in the Latin) are handled correctly.
